one_line: Founder interview with Dragonfly's co-founder and CTO Roman Gershman on why he left AWS ElastiCache to rewrite Redis from scratch, plus the license and language choices behind it.
summary: Better Stack interviews Roman Gershman, co-founder and CTO of DragonflyDB, a Redis-compatible in-memory store. He describes his path from Google Suggest to AWS ElastiCache, and the year-plus internal debate that led him to leave AWS and start Dragonfly. The core technical argument is that incremental multi-threading of Redis (the KeyDB approach, per the captions) still suffers contention on multi-key transactions and Lua scripting, so he chose a full rewrite instead of a fork. He explains keeping the Redis API for ecosystem compatibility, and a source-available license that converts to Apache after four years, reset with each significant release. He also covers choosing C++ over Rust, a lean core team with a hands-on founder, and a roadmap item to use local SSDs as a transparent extension of memory. The host closes by announcing Dragonfly Swarm, which he says combines vertical and horizontal scaling. The content is mostly company history and opinion, with few benchmarks.

key_ideas.idea: Left AWS ElastiCache after more than a year of internal debate, concluding that incremental Redis improvements could not disrupt the market and that real change requires working outside the system.
key_ideas.detail: The argument was that Redis is good software that sometimes fails, and that the proposed improvements were not enough to justify a rewrite. He chose to start his own company.

key_ideas.idea: Rewrote from scratch rather than forking, because incremental multi-threading (KeyDB, per the captions) still ran into lock contention on multi-key transactions and Lua scripting.
key_ideas.detail: He says a full architectural redesign was the only way to cover all use cases with multi-threading, and that the incremental approach led to high contention.

key_ideas.idea: Kept the Redis API on purpose so the client libraries, frameworks and tooling around Redis keep working, and LLMs trained on Redis code also transfer.
key_ideas.detail: Users generally change nothing in their application; some tuning may be needed on the Dragonfly side. The host adds that LLMs' familiarity with the Redis API makes switching easier.

key_ideas.idea: Chose a source-available license with a time-delayed Apache conversion (four years, renewed with each significant release) over plain Apache or AGPL.
key_ideas.detail: The aim is to prevent cloud providers from capitalizing on the code right away while keeping it open for community use. He describes the arrangement as giving the company a four-year development head start on any managed service.

key_ideas.idea: Chose C++ over Rust: he would pick Rust at 20, but at this point learning a new language would cost about two years of building.
key_ideas.detail: He says he has since learned some Rust for another project and liked its package system, but still would not rewrite Dragonfly in it.

key_ideas.idea: Stays deliberately lean and hands-on: the C++ core team is under 10 people within an engineering team of about 20, and the founder answers users directly in GitHub issues and Discord.
key_ideas.detail: He says he wants no middlemen between the company and its users, and credits Redis's Salvatore Sanfilippo for the same approach.

key_ideas.idea: Roadmap focus is making memory cheaper by using local SSDs transparently, so the database uses memory and disk without users managing the split.
key_ideas.detail: He claims local SSDs now respond in tens of microseconds, which is fast enough for users not to notice. No benchmark is given.

key_ideas.idea: Host announces Dragonfly Swarm at the end, which combines vertical and horizontal scaling for terabyte-scale in-memory deployments.
key_ideas.detail: Stated by the host as a recent announcement, not discussed in depth by the founder; no benchmark or architecture details are given.

techniques.name: Rewrite the core instead of forking when the bottleneck is architectural
techniques.how: Founder's reasoning: if a fork adds multi-threading to a single-threaded design, multi-key transactions and Lua scripting still contend on shared state. Redesign the core around the requirements (multi-key transactions, scripting, multi-threading) and keep the external protocol.
techniques.when: A widely used system has an interface your users depend on, but its internals cannot support the concurrency or transaction semantics you need.

techniques.name: Keep the wire API for ecosystem compatibility
techniques.how: Implement the existing protocol and API faithfully and test against the surrounding client libraries and frameworks. Accept some per-deployment tuning on the new backend.
techniques.when: Switching to a new backend for an existing stack, where client libraries, frameworks and LLM-generated code already target the old API.

techniques.name: Time-delayed source-available license
techniques.how: Publish the source under a restrictive license with a fixed date (four years here) after which it converts to Apache. Push the date forward with each significant release.
techniques.when: You want public source access and community use but want to limit managed-cloud competitors during the early years. Note the trade-off: the license is not OSI open source in the interim.

techniques.name: Stay hands-on with the community
techniques.how: The founder answers issues and questions personally on GitHub and Discord instead of routing them through support.
techniques.when: Early-stage open source where direct user feedback drives the roadmap.

tools: Dragonfly Swarm (announced by host, not detailed)
KeyDB (captions read it as KDB; the reference is inferred, not stated)
Google Bigtable and Spanner (mentioned as Google's persistent stores)

numbers.claim: Google Suggest, a real-time, high-scale in-memory service the founder co-designed at Google, around 2007-2008.
Left Google in 2014, and left AWS around 2021 during COVID.
He worked nights without pay for many months while starting Dragonfly.
Dragonfly's source license converts to Apache after four years, renewed with each significant release.
C++ core team under 10 people; overall engineering team about 20.
Local SSDs can return data in dozens of microseconds (founder's claim, no benchmark given).
Learning a new language like Rust would have cost about two years of development time.

hot_takes: Plain Apache or AGPL are both wrong for a database company: Apache leaves it open to cloud competitors, AGPL is too restrictive, so a time-delayed source-available license is the middle ground.
Rewriting the core is better than forking a single-threaded database and adding threads, because the contention problems are architectural.
Choosing a language you already know beats chasing a trendy one like Rust when the goal is to ship a product.

relevance.why: AgentOS uses Redis in its storage layer, and the roadmap includes Redis multi-instance budget counters. Dragonfly is a Redis-compatible alternative, but this interview gives no benchmarks or workload details to justify a switch.
relevance.action: If the Redis budget-counter work goes ahead, benchmark Dragonfly as a drop-in on the actual counter workload, and read its license terms before adopting it.

relevance.why: No overlap with checkpoint/resume, planning, loops, skill ranking or credential handling.
